body:
A vape that fires on its own is annoying at best and worrying at worst. It may buzz in your pocket, drain its battery in a day, make a small clicking sound or produce a puff of vapor when nobody is drawing on it. Auto-firing, sometimes called self-firing or auto-fire, is a known problem with draw-activated devices and, less often, with button-fire devices, and in most cases the cause is simple to find and fix. This guide explains why devices fire on their own, how to tell the causes apart, what to try in order, when to stop using a device and how to prevent it. It is written for adults aged 21 and over. Nicotine is addictive, and nothing here is medical advice. If a device is hot, swollen or smells odd, stop using it at once.

## What auto-firing looks like
- **A light flashing without a draw.**
- **A buzzing or clicking sound.**
- **Vapor appearing from the mouthpiece with no inhale.**
- **A battery that drains much faster than normal.**
- **A device that feels warm in a pocket or bag.**
- **A coil that tastes burnt, because it fired dry.**

## Why it happens
### A sensitive or faulty sensor
Draw-activated devices use a pressure sensor. A sensor that is too sensitive, damaged or contaminated can trigger on tiny pressure changes, or without any. See [auto-draw vs button-fire vapes](/blog/auto-draw-vs-button-fire-vapes/).

### Liquid in the airflow path
A leak can put liquid onto or near the sensor, which can make it trigger or stick. Condensation can do the same.

### Pressure changes
Altitude changes, such as on a plane or in the mountains, can change the pressure in a sealed device and trigger the sensor. Squeezing a device in a bag can do it too.

### Blowing into the mouthpiece
Blowing air across or into a mouthpiece, or a child or pet playing with the device, can trigger it.

### A stuck or damaged button
On button-fire devices, a button that sticks down can fire the device continuously. Lint or liquid around the button can cause this.

### A faulty circuit board or battery
Sometimes the electronics are faulty from new, or damaged by a drop, liquid or heat. This is less common, and it is the reason to stop using a device if basic fixes do not work.

## Step-by-step fixes
1. **Stop using the device and move it to a hard, cool surface, away from anything flammable.**
2. **Check for heat.** If it is hot, swollen or smells odd, do not charge or use it, and take it for recycling. If there is a fire risk, call emergency services.
3. **Remove the pod or tank,** if it is removable, and see if the firing stops.
4. **Check for liquid** in the airflow path and around the contacts and mouthpiece. Wipe with a dry cotton bud. Do not use liquid, and do not blow into the device.
5. **Let it rest** for several hours in a dry place, mouthpiece down on a tissue, in case liquid has drained.
6. **Reseat the pod or tank** and test with a single, gentle draw.
7. **Check the button,** if there is one. Clean around it with a dry cloth, and press it several times to free it.
8. **Check the lock.** Some devices have a lock that prevents firing, usually by clicking the button a set number of times. See [understanding vape device indicator lights](/blog/understanding-vape-device-indicator-lights/).
9. **Try a different pod,** if you have one, to see whether the pod is the cause.
10. **If it still fires, stop using the device,** and contact us.

## Special cases
### On a plane
Pressure changes can trigger devices. Carry them in hand baggage, switched off or locked, with the mouthpiece covered, and do not use them on board. See [traveling with vapes](/blog/traveling-with-vapes-airline-rules/).

### In a bag
Cover the mouthpiece, use a case and keep the device away from heavy items. If the device has a lock, use it.

### With a new device
If a new device fires by itself, it may be faulty. Do not keep using it. Contact us with your order ID and a short video. Opened or used products cannot be returned under our policy, but we will review faulty items on a case-by-case basis through the [refund policy](/refunds/).

## Preventing auto-firing
- **Store devices upright,** with the mouthpiece covered.
- **Keep the airflow path clean.**
- **Do not blow into devices.**
- **Do not squeeze devices in bags.**
- **Use a lock if there is one.**
- **Do not leave devices in heat.**
- **Keep devices away from children and pets.**

## When to stop for good
If a device fires by itself repeatedly after you have cleaned it and reseated the pod, stop using it. A faulty sensor or board will not fix itself, and a device that fires when no one is drawing on it can overheat. Recycle it properly. See [how to dispose of vapes and batteries](/blog/how-to-dispose-of-vapes-and-batteries/).

## A worked example
A customer carries a disposable in a coat pocket, and by midday the battery is flat. They notice a warm patch on the device and a clicking sound. They stop using it, remove it from the pocket and set it on a hard surface. The mouthpiece is damp. They wipe it, leave it overnight and test it the next day. It fires normally on a draw and not otherwise. They cover the mouthpiece in future. The cause was liquid in the airflow, not a faulty device.

## Frequently asked questions in depth
### Is a device that fires by itself dangerous?
It can overheat, so treat it with care. Stop using it if it is hot, swollen or smells odd.

### Can I fix the sensor?
Not at home. Clean and dry the airflow path, and replace the device if the problem continues.

### Why does it only happen in my pocket?
Pressure on the mouthpiece. Cover it, or use a case or a lock.

### Will a new pod fix it?
Sometimes, if the pod is leaking. It will not fix a faulty sensor.

### Can I leave a device charging overnight?
We advise against charging unattended. See our battery care guide.

## Shop
Browse [disposable vapes](/shop/disposables/) and [vape kits](/shop/vape-kits/). All products are for adults aged 21 and over, and nicotine is addictive.

## Checking whether the device is really firing
Before you take apart your routine, confirm that the device is firing at all. Hold it away from your face in a quiet room, and watch the light. If the light flickers without a draw, it is firing. If the battery drains but you see no light, the cause may be standby drain from a nearly flat battery, or a battery that has aged, not auto-firing. Use the device for a day as normal, and note how long the charge lasts. A clear observation tells you whether you are chasing the right problem.

## Environmental causes worth ruling out
Ceiling fans, air conditioning vents and car vents can blow across a mouthpiece and trigger a very sensitive sensor. So can wind when you walk outside with the mouthpiece facing forward. Try holding the device with the mouthpiece pointing down or away, or covering it with a cap. If the firing stops, the sensor is sensitive but working, and a cap or a case is the practical fix.

## What a repair is not
Do not open a sealed device. Do not try to bend, clean or replace the sensor. Do not apply heat, alcohol or other liquids. Do not charge a device that has been wet. These steps can damage the electronics and the battery, and they create a risk of overheating. If a device is faulty, replace it, and recycle the old one. See [how to dispose of vapes and batteries](/blog/how-to-dispose-of-vapes-and-batteries/).

## Contacting us
If a new device fires by itself, tell us through the [contact page](/contact/). Please include your order ID, the product name, how long the problem has lasted, a short video of the light or the behavior and what you have already tried. This helps us decide the best way to help, in line with our [refund policy](/refunds/). Do not send the device until we ask, and keep it in a cool, secure place away from children and pets until we do.

## Long-term habits
Treat every device as a small battery with electronics, and give it the care you would give a phone. Keep it clean, dry and cool, and cover the mouthpiece when it is not in use. Charge it on a hard surface, unplug it when full and replace it if it shows signs of damage. These habits prevent most problems, including auto-firing.

## Using a lock or a cap as a permanent fix
If your device is working normally apart from firing in your bag, there is nothing wrong that needs repair. Use the lock whenever you put it away, and a small silicone cap or a case on the mouthpiece. Many adults keep a case that holds the device upright, which protects the sensor and keeps liquid from pooling. It costs little, it extends battery life and it removes a common annoyance. If the device has no lock, a case is the best option.

## Keeping a record
If a device is under warranty or covered by our policy, a record of what happened helps. Note the date it started, what you saw and what you tried. Take a short video of the behavior. This lets us understand the problem quickly, and it is more reliable than memory.

faq.q: Why does my vape fire by itself?
faq.a: Common causes are a sensitive or faulty sensor, liquid in the airflow path, pressure on the mouthpiece, a stuck button or a faulty circuit.
Stop using it, set it on a hard, cool surface and check it for heat. If it is hot, swollen or smells odd, do not use or charge it.

faq.q: How do I clean the airflow path?
faq.a: Wipe the mouthpiece and contacts with a dry cotton bud and let the device rest. Do not use liquid or blow into the device.

faq.q: Can pressure on a plane cause it?
faq.a: Yes. Carry devices in hand baggage, switched off or locked, with the mouthpiece covered.

faq.q: When should I stop using it?
faq.a: If it keeps firing after cleaning and reseating, or if it is hot or damaged. Recycle it properly.

faq.q: Who do I contact about a faulty new device?
faq.a: Use the contact page with your order ID and a short video. Our refund policy explains what applies.
